chunks.sectionTitle: Reliability, v alidity, u tility, and u sage
chunks.content:
INTERPRETATION
Figure 40.1 A Conceptual Framework Bus Architecture.
C h APT e R 40 n a Guide to Resea R ch n n n 513
research study may be briefly defined as an index measuring the degree of agreement among
re-observations of the same phenomena. Unreliability therefore implies variation among
re-observations.
Two additional distinct concepts that should not be confused with reliability and validity
are utility and usage. The utility of a concept may be defined as the correlation coefficient
between the use of the concept and the efficiency of controlling its relevant phenomena. The
definition of usage is to measure the proportion of a specified group which uses the concept
or uses it in a specified way.
Note that it is possible to take usage as a criterion for validating a concept. Also utility of
a concept actually means how well it contributes to our ability to predict and control phe-
nomena. Many times in science, a concept is useful or useless in proportion to its ability to
enable prediction and control of relevant phenomena better than with alternative concepts
or absence of them.
In the physical science component of the field of computing, utility would seem to be the
most important of the four properties. Reliability clearly would be next, while validity and
usage are desirable but of less importance in the long run for scientific progress.
In summary the four properties imply that researchers should ask:
1. Are the results in the current research study useful for prediction?
2. Are the procedures employed reliable?
3. How valid are the results by specified criteria?
4. How widely used is the concept?

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.4 The Scientific Method
chunks.content:
40.4 The Scientific Method
Any one who has taken a physical science class in their formal education has been exposed
to the scientific method. Basically, it is a sequence of steps undertaken to find the answers to
proposed questions. Physical scientist formulate questions and seek to find answers to these
questions employing the following regimental set of steps:
1. Conduct research and observation of the phenomena.
2. Identify the problem.
3. State the formal hypothesis.
4. Conduct the experiment.
5. Analyze the results and draw conclusions.
But how does the following of these steps differ from solving the problem using common sense?
First: The scientific method systematically builds their theoretical structures, tests them for
internal consistency, and subjects them to empirical testing. The average person may use
conceptual schemes and theories, but usually only in a loose fashion.
514 n n n Resea R ch Methods fo R i nfo RM ation s yste M s n C hAPT e R 40
Second: Scientists systematically and empirically test their theories and hypotheses. The
average person also tests hypotheses, but does so in a selective fashion.
Third: There is a profound difference in the application of control. Scientists take deliberate
steps, the average person would simply overlook, to control their explanations of observed
phenomena in a systematic manner.
Fourth: Laymen simply invoke common sense for their explanations among phenomena.
Scientists cultivate relations, they consciously and systematically pursue relations.
Fifth: When attempting to explain the observed phenomena the scientist rules out meta-
physical explanations, which tend to be the layman’s mainstay.
In summary, science is concerned with things that can be observed and tested.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.4.1 Research
chunks.content:
40.4.1 Research
Often the first step in research in most graduate programs is to request that the student
perform a background search to identify at least 3 to 6 potential questions. In other words,
have the student begin to develop a research area. Clearly, the student as any professional
researcher might be influenced by past experiences which could enhance their research
studies. In particular, their past interests and experiences help them to identify particular
concepts to consider in the actual pursuit of a new problem.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.4.2 Problem
chunks.content:
40.4.2 Problem
Usually the first draft of the problem is stated in ordinary prose and their rationale presented
in the form of an argument. First, the researcher may experience doubt when observing
the phenomena. Next, the researcher formulates the problem. They study the literature
and internet accessible resources, seek the experiences of others, and draw upon their own
experiences. Once the basic question is formulated, then the hypothesis is constructed and,
ultimately, implications are deduced empirically. The hypothesis is tested by observation and
experimentation. On the basis of the research evidence, the hypothesis is either rejected or
it will fail to be rejected.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.4.3 Project experimentation
chunks.content:
40.4.3 Project experimentation
In this phase of the research process the hypothesis is tested usually under the setting of
a well controlled experiment. A design is either developed or chosen compatible with the
research hypothesis and the question being tested, that controls or equalizes the effect of
as many important extraneous variables as feasible. The design should also randomize the
effects of all uncontrolled factors. Then the changes taking place in the dependent variable
are observed by making changes in the independent variables.
The essential characteristics of a good project experimentation are:
1. An experimental design is used that insures that the observed dependent variable
effects are unbiased estimates of the true effects.
C h APT e R 40 n a Guide to Resea R ch n n n 515
2. A quantitative description of the precision of the dependent variable effects can be
regarded as estimates of the true effects.
3. According to the broader purposes of the experiment the observed dependent vari-
able effects will have whatever degree of precision that is required.
4. The hypothesis is a reliable and valid test.
5. The design can satisfy the requirements at minimum “cost.”
During this phase researchers should ask:
What are the available resources?
What are the constraints which “time” may have for the completion of the study?
What is the actual “goodness” of a design, or are the internal and external validities of
the experiment met?

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.4.4 Project conclusion
chunks.content:
40.4.4 Project conclusion
In the last part of the experiment the researcher is to interpret, conclude and make recom-
mendations for further research. Results achieved should be compared with:
1. studies previously reviewed,
2. the conceptual framework within which the research was conducted, and
3. studies that may not have been previously considered but are suggested by the
outcomes.
For more information on the scientific method the interested reader should consult The
Scientific Method found at http://oiscl.net/scientific_Method.pdf.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.5 Topic Research
chunks.content:
40.5 Topic Research
How do researcher come up with an idea for a research project? The anthropologist often
comes up with ideas by being actively engaged in field work. These ideas are a result of see-
ing what has been happening in the field.
Background reviews, as discussed, allow one to extend and refine previous research. Addi-
tionally, many organizations publish Requests for Proposals (RFPs). RFPs usually describe
the problem, the context in which it operates, the desired approach for investigating the
problem, and the amount the organization would be willing to pay for the research. Based
upon the researcher’s educational background, culture, and experiences, the researcher
needs to check the proposed problem for whether or not the problem is feasible.
A good reference on topic research is found at http://www.socialresearchmethods.net/kb/
probfrm.php.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.6 Project Research
chunks.content:
40.6 Project Research
What is the purpose of a research report? Clearly it is used to tell the readers the problem
investigated, the methods used to solve the problem, the results of the investigation, and the
conclusions inferred from the results. As expeditiously and clearly as possible, the report
should inform the reader what was done, why it was done, the outcome of doing it, and the
investigator’s conclusions. The reader should be able to reach his own conclusions regarding
the adequacy of the research and the validity of the reported results and conclusions.
The general structure of the research report is the same as the structure of the research
itself:
i. Problem
a. Theory, hypotheses, definitions
b. Previous research, the background review
ii. Methodology [Data Collection]
a. Sample and sampling method
b. How hypotheses were tested [methodology], experimental procedures,
instrumentation
c. Measurement of variables
d. Methods of analysis, statistics
e. Pretesting and pilot studies
iii. Results, Interpretations and Conclusions
In project research the problem section differs from that usually found in a thesis. In a
thesis it is usually long and detailed, while in a research report it is kept to a minimum. The
researcher needs to:
1. tell the reader what the research problem is about in a question form.
2. state the general problem not in a precise and operational manner, but simply set the
general stage for the reader. Sub-problems should be precise and contain implica-
tions for testing. Some researchers state the general and specific hypotheses in an
effort to inform the reader of the main area of investigation and the specific proposi-
tions that were tested.
All variables should be operationally defined. Every effort should be made to inform the
reader not only of the variables but also what they mean. These operational terms must be
given justification.
C h APT e R 40 n a Guide to Resea R ch n n n 517

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.7 Scientific w riting
chunks.content:
40.7 Scientific w riting
A research report must be written with clarity and accuracy. After all, the report must be
informative. Efforts at generating emotion, to entertain, or to persuade are to be avoided. As
a result the report should be written in a fashion similar to an military officer giving orders
to the troops, a modified version for research report writing includes:
1. Keep it SIMPLE.
2. Operationally define all terms.
3. Start with the goal, the problem statement.
4. Use simple words which avoid usage of jargon.
5. Write in the third person with a passive voice.
6. Normally speak to the reader in past tense, except for usage of the present tense for
specific directions to the reader.
7. Avoid exclusionary and stereotyping in writing.
8. Eliminate all unnecessary words, sentences, and paragraphs.
9. Find a peer reviewer for your report.
10. Write the abstract last. It includes primarily the main points but factually and briefly
stated. This is not a summary.
11. Maintain the practice of critical examination of others writing. Practice, thought,
and study of the ‘good, bad, and ugly’ of others writing is mandatory.
12. An exception to (2) is used infrequently to free up the dryness of the report by using
the active voice in the first person and using the appropriate tense.
For additional information, for researchers in the computing field, about better writing con-
sult the Chicago Style American Psychological Association (APA) publication manual.
An excellent list of questions for evaluating a research report is Guidelines for Critiquing
Research Articles found at http://www.sonoma.edu/users/n/nolan/n400/critique.htm.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.8 Matters of e thical Concern in Research
chunks.sectionTitle: Matters of e thical Concern in Research
chunks.content:
40.8 Matters of e thical Concern in Research
Computer professionals are keenly aware of professional codes of ethics, behavioral guide-
lines, and professional responsibility since their professional organizations have codes of pro-
fessional conduct as well as self-assessments on ethical issues in computing. The main ones
are the ACM and IEEE Computer Society. Jointly they developed the Software Engineering
Code of Ethics and Professional Practice. A Code of Ethics for Research emphasizes some
518 n n n Resea R ch Methods fo R i nfo RM ation s yste M s n C hAPT e R 40
of the same issues addressed by the latter codes of conduct: ethical issues of honesty and
fairness, responsibility to respect confidentiality, maintenance of professional competence,
being aware of relevant laws, and honoring contracts and agreements. Additional stress is
placed upon: responsibility to respect property and protect privacy, avoid harming others,
and respecting property rights.
The University of Pittsburgh offers the following guidelines, GUIDELINES FOR RESPON-
SIBLE CONDUCT OF RESEARCH by the Office of Research Integrity, Office of Research
Integrity (2007) found at http://www.pitt.edu/~provost/ethresearch.html.
40.9 e xercises
1. Explain the relationship that exists between being able to generalize and replicate in
a research project.
2. Complete a background search to operationally define face validity, content validity,
criterion-related validity, translation validity, predictive validity, concurrent validity,
convergent validity, and discriminant validity.
3. Complete a background search on how to operationally define ex-post facto experi-
mentation. How does this approach differ from a true experiment?
4. Explain how reliability and validity are related.
5. Establish your own conceptual framework for research adapted to your field of inter-
est in which you will carry out investigations. Try to demonstrate that your conceptual
framework has potential as a meta-analysis tool by fulfilling the conditions set for it.
By the criteria outlined in this chapter, determine if it can be judged to be a useful
research tool in the context for which it was developed. These are the criteria that any
researcher should satisfy regardless of the simplicity or complexity of the framework
being evaluated.
6. Suppose you plan to test the hypothesis that a push information method to the sales
force of your company enhances the overall company sales production by increasing
the sales force’s understanding of the client base. Outline an ideal research design
to test this hypothesis, assuming you have complete command of the situation and
plenty of money and help. Set up an alternate design as follows:
n A design with complete randomization
n A matching design with complete randomization

Now compromise the ideal. Set up alternative designs as follows:
n A matching design without randomization
n A compromise design
How do these four designs compare in their control power? Which design do you think
should best test the hypothesis? In which design can you put the greatest faith? Why?
C h APT e R 40 n a Guide to Resea R ch n n n 519
7. A college faculty group is to study a core curriculum program instituted during the
previous year. All incoming freshmen are required to take this program. Discuss the
problems and difficulties the researchers face. How much faith can be put in their
findings?
8. The faculty of a university school of business decides to begin a core curriculum for
all undergraduates and, therefore needs, to study the effectiveness of the proposed
curriculum. A faculty research group is asked to study the program for two years. The
research group, wishing to have a group with which to compare the core curriculum
group, requests that the regular program be continued for two years and that stu-
dents be allowed to volunteer for the core program or the regular program. In this
way, the group feels it will have an experimental group and a control group. Discuss
the group’s proposal critically. Would you have faith in its findings at the end of the
two years? Give reasons for reacting positively or negatively to the proposal. What
research design would you like to set up?
9. Imagine that you are a graduate school professor and that you are asked to judge the
worth of a proposed doctoral thesis. The doctoral student is a database administrator
who is instituting a new type of administration into his company’s system. He plans
to study the effects of the new administration for a three-year period and then write
his thesis. To keep the study objective, he will not study any other company situation.
Discuss the candidate’s proposal, keeping these questions in mind: If the study is com-
pleted, should he be awarded the degree? Is such a study suitable for doctoral work?

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.10 Project
chunks.content:
40.10 Project
i ntroduction
Little is known of the strategies that researchers adopt during the process of conducting a
project, especially in the computing field. You are to conduct a study that contributes to the
knowledge of that process by posing the research question: “What are the influencing fac-
tors on the research process and how do researchers harness these factors to enhance their
research?” The majority of textbooks on research methods in business, education, and the
behavioral sciences follow the template for research discussed in Section 40.4, The Scientific
Method. Feel free to use this template. The second stage, identifying the problem, should be
expanded to include preliminary data and negotiating access and ethical issues.
A succession of interviews needs to be conducted with eight or more academic profession-
als in either information systems, computer science, or computer engineering to construct a
preliminary model of their perception of the research process.
You are to collect data on this recommended factors and to provide a structured way of
assessing an individual’s perception of the research process.
The majority of textbooks on business, social science, and educational research detail the
research process. The preliminary stage of identifying the research problem should be
expanded to incorporate preliminary data gathering and negotiating access and ethical issues.
520 n n n Resea R ch Methods fo R i nfo RM ation s yste M s n C hAPT e R 40
Little has been written on the issues arising at these different stages of the research process.
Factors that affect research projects are knowledge, skills, and personal background.
The following list of factors can be constructed, but feel free to modify:
n Motivation
n IT skills
n Financial resources
n Time availability
n Intellectual skills
n Administrative skills
n Creativity
n Communication skills
n Library resources
n Research knowledge
n Perseverance
n Business knowledge

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 40.11 Problem Solving
chunks.content:
40.11 Problem Solving
Conduct this survey research study and report the results. Consider selecting interviewees
all from the same university but at different stages in their career as an experimental con-
trol. All interviewees selected should have had at least one example of their work appearing
in conference proceedings or refereed journals within the last two years, a second form of
experimental control. The interviewees should represent a variety of computing disciplines:
networking, database, information systems, computer graphics, operating systems, etc. Fur-
ther interviews should be conducted with each participant that examines their experiences
and the importance of the various research stages and the impact of the various factors. The
participants will then be asked to delete any influencing factors they considered unimportant
and to add any influencing factors that they considered important. The aggregate results of
the interviews should be compiled and analyzed.

41.1 lntroduction
Recall the last time you applied for a job. At one point you probably filled out an employ-
ment application. This instrument is the organization’s effort to collect information directly
from the group of candidates for the job. Notice this process involves obtaining information
directly from the participants in the study by asking questions.
But what type of information is collected? When you report your age, gender, years of edu-
cation, and income on the application these response values are facts. Facts are values that
can independently be verified. In addition to facts, often these employment applications
contain questions to prompt the respondent’s preference, feeling, or behavioral intention.
These type of questions are referred to as opinions. For example, How would you react
to the scenario X? or If Y responded to X in manner Z, rate your degree of agreement/dis-
agreement. Primarily facts differ from opinions with respect to how they are operationally
defined. A birth date field data value can be used to capture the respondent’s age with little
or no controversy. But how we capture, implement, or interpret opinions can and probably
would generate considerable controversy. Finally, a question like: How many times have you
attended X? are referred to as behavior, or actions completed by the respondent.
Often surveys include all three of these types of content. Opinions can be objectively mea-
sured but cannot be verified. At the same time, facts can be verified. Behavior can be verified,
although facts are usually easier to verify. The point being made is that, without verification,
there is a tendency to apply Garbage-In-Garbage-Out to your research.
This chapter’s purpose is to introduce several issues and procedures of survey research. Any
research study in which participants are directly asked questions, which might be using ques-
tionnaires or interviews, to obtain information is referred to as survey research. Note that,
a study is not referred to as survey research simply because it employs questionnaires or
interviews. The study is a survey research if information is obtained directly from a group
of individuals. Survey research is highly valuable when one recognizes that it accommodates
large sample sizes, even with the possibility of being efficient at acceptable “costs.”
41.2 t ypes of s urveys
In this section we will view and examine different types of surveys. Generally, these consist
of questionnaires and interviews. Questionnaires can be classified as: mail surveys, e-surveys,
and group administered surveys.
A Mail Survey is a survey in which the respondent completes the survey instrument without

intervention from the researcher.
E-surveys are either E-mail surveys or Web-mail surveys.
A Group-Administered Survey is where a group of participants are brought together and are
asked to respond to a set of structured questions in a survey instrument handed out to each
person to complete within a specific time.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 41.2.1 Questionnaires
chunks.content:
41.2.1 Questionnaires
Most surveys use structured instructions to ensure that the participants understand how to
properly complete the instrument. Even though mail surveying is appealing, one must keep
in mind that they tend to have low response rates.
The difference between E-mail and Web-mail surveys is due to how the communication
links are utilized. E-mail surveys are “pushed” directly to the respondent’s computer and
Web mail surveys are “pulled” by the respondent from the Web site. As attractive as these
types of surveys are the researcher needs to consider whether or not the ‘have - and - have -
not’ syndrome (not all participants might have access to E-mail or Web-mail) applies to the
participants in the study.
Questionnaires are often convenient for group settings and thus enable high response rates.
When administrating the questionnaire, the researcher, due to being present, can respond to
respondents questions about the study and get clarification on completing the questionnaire.
41.2.2 i nterviews
Classification for interviews includes: face-to-face interviews, focused-interviewing, and tele-
phone interviewing.
Face-to-face interviews are where the survey instrument is orally administered.
Focused Interviews usually provide the interviewer with highly structured predetermined
primary questions but allow flexibility to the interviewer in asking secondary questions.
Telephone interviewing is simply an alternative to face-to-face interviews employing tele-
communications technology.
In face-to-face interviews where the instrument itself is orally administered the interview
must be highly structured. The interviewer must: provide instructions, record responses,
and answer respondents’ questions. From this list of activities it becomes apparent that inter-
viewers should probably be trained and certified.
Focused interviews tend to generate research studies with a high degree of internal and
external validity. But an unfocused interview, where participants are allowed to openly dis-
cuss a topic often obtained by the interviewer probing the participant, thereby rendering
questionable internal and external validity for the interview and study. This type of interview
tends to be expensive but at the same time enlightening and extremely effective.
To determine which method to use, the researcher needs to address the population, sam-
pling, the question, content, bias, and administrative issues. A overview of survey research by
the Public Administration Program at North Carolina State University can be found at http://
faculty.chas.ncsu.edu/garson/PA765/survey.htm.
Whatever method of research, in this case survey research, the researcher must strive for
reliability and validity. The interested reader should consult the following articles supported

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 41.2.1 Questionnaires
chunks.content:
by Colorado State University (2011) found at http://writing.colostate.edu/guides/research/
relvaal/pop2a.cfm.
524 n n n r e S earch Metho DS F or In F or M at I on Sy S te MS n ch apter 41
41.2.3 w riting your own survey questions
Reconsider the employment application. What is the basic format of this instrument? It
contains item topics [personal data, position applying for, record of education, etc.], instruc-
tions [how to respond], item formats [birth date as 1/23/43], and arrangements of items. All
of these components can have an effect on the information obtained.
A few helpful question writing considerations include:
1. BE NEAT! This is partially accomplished with spacing.
2. Make sure that interviewers and participants fully understand the purpose of the
study and how to correctly complete the survey.
3. Be careful with wording and labels. Avoid slang and jargon.
4. Place sensitive items at the end of sections to reduce response bias.
5. Place nonthreatening and interesting items at the beginning of sections.
6. Start the instrument with a purpose of study statement followed by the general
instructions needed to correctly respond. Next include the personal demographic
section.
7. Visually set off each section, a group of interrelated questions, with spacing and
indentations.
8. Remember that item order can both create and eliminate response bias.
9. Consider required response rate, acceptable costs, item types, and item formats
needed during the design phase with a keen eye on analysis to be employed.
10. Fine tune the instrument and prepare interviewers through pretesting. Use pretest-
ing to investigate every aspect of the survey project.
This is only a short list of the considerations required when designing your own instrument
or interview. The interested reader should consult Outline on Research Instruments found
at http://www2.uvawise.edu/pww8y/Resources/MERes/ResInstruments/00ResInstruments.
html. The University of Central Florida publishes an article, Writing Your Own Survey
Questions, found at http://www.fctl.ucf.edu/ResearchAndScholarship/SoTL/creatingSoTL-
Projects/implementingmanaging/writeyourownsurveyitems.php#general
It is evident that there are many formats and styles for survey instruments. The researcher
needs to choose an instrument by comparing the advantages and disadvantages for the dif-
ferent types of surveys. But the best advice is to remember the old computer slogan GIGO,
Garbage-In-Garbage-Out. If you start by immediately designing and implementing your
own instrument, then your work is just beginning. You will need to determine the instru-
ments’ reliability and validity, a task worthy of a whole new textbook devoted to only that
issue. Commercial and professional instruments are available for most research domains,

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 41.2.1 Questionnaires
chunks.content:
complete with results of their reliability and validity analyzes. Start by searching for an
appropriate existing survey instrument. Do not design your own instrument unless abso-
lutely necessary.

Study Comparative Study of Graduate Information Systems and MBA Students Cognitive
Styles, by King and Stock found on this book’s companion DVD. Problem-solving styles are
critical dimensions in corporate decision making. In order to study the comparative prob-
lem-solving styles of college graduate students majoring in information systems versus busi-
ness administration, the Kirton Adaption-Innovation Inventory (KAI) was used to determine
the cognitive styles of the students enrolled in the Master of Science in Information Systems
(MSIS) and the Master of Business Administration (MBA) programs at the University of
Mary Hardin-Baylor (UMHB) during the Spring semester of 2007. The results of the study
were also analyzed by demographic variants.

41.4 s ampling
In most survey research studies the instrument or interview will be administered to a sample
of the population. The analysis is done on a sample, or a subset of the population. Actually,
samples are selected from a sampling frame, or a published listing of the elements in the
population. Generally, sampling is a valuable tool for obtaining data quickly, cheaply and
accurately. The purpose of this section is to define and illustrate some of the more common
sampling methods. Also discussed is the difference between two major types of sampling
procedures: probability and non-probability sampling.
Suppose a sign manufacturer has produced over 1000 signs and wants to determine average
packaging weight for various groupings of signs. To solve this problem, focus on a small scale
of the problem by considering a population consisting of 24 signs: 8 octagons, 6 pentagons,

Notice that the most precise results under cluster sampling, as suggested by comparing the
compositions of clusters 1 and 2, will be obtained when each cluster has a heterogeneous
composition, while the clusters tend to be similar. The estimate derived from stratified sam-
pling was near the true value of the population parameter because the units in each cluster
were all mixed up while similarity was maintained between clusters. The reverse is true for
stratified clustering, strata are internally homogeneous, while the strata themselves are as
heterogeneous as possible.
In practice, cluster sampling produces less precise estimates than a simple random sample of
the same size, since in actual studies one is often required to accept the clusters as they exist.
Usually these clusters will be relatively homogeneous.
Suppose the researcher wants to determine the type of activity and average time spent on
computing in the home on a daily basis. Image the potential cost of running this study using a
simple random sample. Why not use cluster sampling? Households in a single book are fairly

block to block. Then a sample of a large number of neighborhoods containing thousands of
households, cluster sampling; might provide as accurate a result as a widely dispersed simple
random sample of half as many households, but at much lower cost. While the simple random
sample is more precise, practically with respect to size, the larger cluster sample will be cost

41.4.4 a lternative sampling methods
There are other sampling methods employed in practice. The following brief list provides
operational definitions for the alternative methods.
41.4.4.1 s ystematic s ampling
For the population of signs we would simply select a random number between 1 and int
(n/N), where n is the sample size, N is the population size, and int(_) is the largest positive
whole number less than or equal to the function’s argument. Then choose every int (n/N)
sampling unit from a starting point, say a value between 1 and n. Systematic random sam-
pling is based upon the concept of selecting elements from a randomly arranged sampling
frame according to ordered criteria. For a very large sampling frame and a large sample,
systematic random sampling is very inexpensive and direct plus very simple to implement.
41.4.4.2 d ouble s ampling
In the quest for a more cost effective and efficient sampling method for situations requiring
large samples and large sampling frames, a sample of a sample can be employed, or dou-
ble sampling can be used. For instances, a simple brief questionnaire could be utilized for
obtaining data on representative household occupations for a large population from a sample
of ten thousands of households. This process could then be administered a comprehensive
questionnaire, using the proportions of each occupational group in the larger sample, for
selecting a sample with sample size in the several orders of magnitude lower than for the
first questionnaire.
All of the sampling methods discussed so far rely on obtaining a random sample, there-
fore, you can rely on the Central Limit Theorem and the associated properties of the unit
normal distribution to determine the amount of sampling error in the sample. In order to
calculate the standard error, or the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of means,
it is necessary to evaluate the formula:

included in the sample, it is called nonprobability sampling methods. Without a sampling

Think about the person-on-the-street interviews seen on local and national newscasts. In
accidental sampling sample units are selected on the basis of being available or being easily
included upon immediate selection.
Most of us have run into people in a mall carrying clipboards with attached questionnaires
stopping various people entering or leaving the mall. Usually, the mall pedestrian is pursued
by these people and asked to participate in some study; actually the mall pedestrian has been
sized up to see whether or not they are qualified for being selected for membership in the
sample. Purposive Sampling is useful in situations requiring efficient access to a target group.
Modal sampling is when you sample the most frequent case. Interviews of the ‘typical voter’
is an example of a modal sampling application. But what is a ‘typical voter’?
Panel of experts are common at national and /or professional meetings. This is a good
approach to elicit the views of individuals with specific expertise. Expert Sampling deals
with assembling a sample of individuals possessing demonstrable experience and/or exper-
tise within a domain.
Pollsters use quota sampling to predict the outcomes of elections. The sampling units are
selected on the basis of perceived categories within the population. In stratified sampling
the sampling elements are selected within the stratified groups. On the other hand, in quota
sampling the elements are selected within presumed subdivisions of the population.
41.5 s ampling e rrors
When sampling ensures that every sampling unit has a chance of being selected and the prob-
ability of selection is known, then the sampling errors are controllable. The following list points
out some important types that the researcher needs to be concerned about when gathering data:
1. reporting and processing errors,
2. non-response errors,
3. errors in sample selection, and unit sampling errors.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 41.6 Field s tudies
chunks.content:
41.6 Field s tudies
Imagine being asked to implement research on everyday events. For example, assume you
have been hired to study the cognitive activities of professional programmers in their corpo-
rate computing center.
How would you begin this study? What are we really trying to accomplish? We are attempt-
ing to understand how they resolve and solve problems during their daily activities, both on
an individual and team basis. What type of organizational structures formally and informally
are in place within the working environment?
It will probably take a considerable amount of effort to simply decide which aspects of the
personnel’s behavior to investigate, let alone determine hypotheses to test. These behaviors
involve individual and corporate team interactions.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: chapter 41 n Survey an D F I el D r e S earch n n n 531
chunks.content:
chapter 41 n Survey an D F I el D r e S earch n n n 531
But how will we collect all this information? Based upon most of our everyday experiences
many of us would probably suspect:
1. use of photography to capture photos that can be immediately shared and analyzed.
2. take photographs every day of a sitting or artifact possibly photographs every day of a
team’s whiteboard – which could contain a list, or log, of an individual’s assignments
and other personnel with whom they interact.
3. use of video for recording meetings for future interpretation.
4. maintain written notes – a pocket notebook to use on a moments notice, a word
processor to organize your thoughts using an “outline” mode or writing observations
under continual recording and maintenance.
5. you could classify the systematically organized observations.
Basically, you would be starting to employ a collection of methods that include direct obser-
vation of naturally occurring events. Direct observation is where the event is observed as it
happens. Naturally occurring events are events that are not created, sustained, or discontin-
ued solely for research purposes. This type of research is referred to as Field Research. In
this section, the practices of field research will be discussed.
Through observation you would begin to collect data on the personnel’s activities and even-
tually formulate new hypotheses. Field research is suitable for exploratory and descriptive
goal finding studies.
Most of your time during a field study is bound to be through either recall or direct observa-
tion. In the proposed study, you would be examining how people solve problems and make
decisions in real work environments. By studying the daily events of the personnel in this
work environment, it would be best for you to not only observe but simultaneously, take part
in the events. After all, the best approach to understand problem solving, is to ‘learn it by
doing it’. This approach is called Participant Observation. Studies where you observe events
without participating in them, thus being as unobtrusive as possible, are called Systematic
Observation.
During the proposed study, it seems appropriate to collect data on observations of behavior
on the part of the software development team. However, imagine the insight to be gained by
collecting their individual reports of behavior.
Systematic information on the personnel’s daily activities could be obtained simply by asking
them to report their activities for a recent specified period of time. You could ask them open-
ended questions and record the answers, or create a time diary. Clearly, both of these tech-
niques require interviewing and recording skills. The time diary would keep data on when
an activity starts, ends, and its sequence with the other daily activities. More than likely for

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: chapter 41 n Survey an D F I el D r e S earch n n n 531
chunks.content:
your recording in the time diary, you will need to invent a coding scheme for the activities.
But when do you record the activities? The obvious answer is to record the subject’s behav-
ior the moment they are observed. This type of procedure is referred to as Instantaneous
Sampling.
532 n n n r e S earch Metho DS F or In F or M at I on Sy S te MS n ch apter 41
Just like it is important for students to take notes, participant observers must decide how
much detail to include in their field journals. If something happens, then you must post it in
the field journal. How often should you maintain the field journal? The obvious answer is at
every available opportunity. Often the difference between remembering and forgetting an
event is dependent on sketch notes in the field journal. Remember that the field journal is
the participant observer’s primary research tool.
Clearly field research involves the researcher following activities and observing through
questionnaires and interviewing. These events must be selected, recorded, coded, and inter-
preted. The field study is really an understanding process, both about the domain and about
the cognitive activities under study. The researcher wants to:
1. form hypotheses about the behavioral patterns observed,
2. make predictions, and
3. finally, verify the predictions.
The following article ‘The Observational Study of Behavior’, by J. Altmann published in
Behavior 48: 1–41, illustrates how data analysis of abstractions and the associated interpreta-
tions can be the primary effort in a field study. When studying this article it is important to try
to identify sources of error in the study. Observations need to be measured reliably, or con-
sistently, and they must be valid, in other words, do they measure what they are supposed to
measure. Otherwise you cannot describe events and test hypotheses about them. Inadequate
sampling could be present in a field study. Also the researcher should be very careful about
changing their minds about what to observe, this leads to inadequate sampling. Other error
sources are due to recording, observing, and interpreting observations.
A text on qualitative field research which serves as a manual to follow when conducting an
ethnographic project, complete with examples, is A Guide to Qualitative Field Research by
Carol Bailey published by Pine Forge Press, 2nd Edition (September 14, 2006). Another
reference, for the interested reader is The Observational Study of Behavior by J. Altmann
published in Behavior 48: 1–41.

chunks.content:
41.7 Field r esearch e xample
Study Ethnographic Study of MSIS Student Project Team Dynamics, by Ronald S. King,
found on the textbook’s DVD. Problem-solving styles and interpersonal dynamics of project
teams are often critical dimensions of the ability of a team to function effectively. In order
to study the problem-solving styles of students enrolled in a graduate Database Adminis-
tration and Development class at the University of Mary Hardin-Baylor (UMHB) and to
track their intrateam interactions, the theory established by M.J. Kirton in 1976 was used
to determine the cognitive styles of the students. Students were categorized according to
adaption-innovation characteristics of the Kirton Adaption-Innovation Inventory. These cat-
egorizations were then applied to interpret the results of interviews from informants and the
team leaders, and about the abilities of project team members to work and communicate
with each other.
